```{r setup}
#| include: false
# Figures come from scripts/90_report_figs.R (figs/<figure>_<profile>.png + manifest.csv).
# The CONUS ("full") version of a figure is shown when it exists, otherwise the dev one.
figs <- if (file.exists("figs/manifest.csv")) {
  utils::read.csv("figs/manifest.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
} else data.frame(figure = character(), profile = character())

show_fig <- function(name, caption, alt = caption) {
  m <- figs[figs$figure == name, , drop = FALSE]
  pick <- intersect(c("full", "dev"), m$profile)
  pick <- pick[file.exists(sprintf("figs/%s_%s.png", name, pick))]
  if (!length(pick)) {
    cat(sprintf('\n::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}\n## Figure pending\n%s\n:::\n\n',
                caption))
    return(invisible())
  }
  r <- m[m$profile == pick[1], ][1, ]
  note <- sprintf("[%s · %s · figure made %s]{.fig-meta}", r$extent, r$years, r$made)
  cat(sprintf('\n![%s %s](figs/%s_%s.png){#fig-%s fig-alt="%s" .column-page-right}\n\n',
              caption, note, name, pick[1], gsub("_", "-", name), alt))
}
```

## Work in progress
This page is updated as the analysis runs. Results are preliminary and will change.
It is a companion to the [fuel phenology regions page](index.html).
:::

## At a glance

**The question.** Curing is the fuel variable fire managers care about most for grasses, and
the U.S. has almost no ground record of it. USA National Phenology Network (NPN) observers
record, for tagged grass plants, what share of the plant is still green, several times a
month. This study asks what that record shows: when grasses green up and cure, where and
for which grass types, how much those dates change from year to year, and whether weather
explains the early and late years.

**How it fits the regions work.** The [regions page](index.html) builds typical green-up
and curing dates for every 4 km cell and tested weather rules against satellite dates; most
of those rules lost their skill when checked at NPN grass sites. This study works the other
way round: it starts from the ground dates and asks what can be predicted from weather at
all. It is the validation dataset for the typical-date product and for any future
ground-fitted rules.

**Questions.**

1. **The record:** how many sites, species, years and plants carry usable curves, and where?
2. **Climatology:** typical green-up, curing and cured dates for cool-season (C3) and
   warm-season (C4) grasses, by region.
3. **Place versus year:** how much of each date is fixed by place, and how much varies from
   year to year? Is the year-to-year part shared among plants and sites?
4. **Climate across space:** do typical dates follow each site's climate?
5. **Weather from year to year:** how far up a ladder of models, from one driver to a random
   forest, does it take to explain a grass's early and late years?
6. **Is simple enough?** Where do simple process rules sit on that ladder?

**What we have found so far (October 2026).**

- **The record is mostly NEON.** 6,331 plant-years of percent-green curves (1,617 plants,
  130 sites, 70 species, 2014–2024). 94 % come from 36 National Ecological Observatory
  Network field sites, where technicians follow five tagged plants per species in natural
  plots; the other 94 sites add spatial coverage but few years each.
- **Typical green-up follows site climate; typical curing much less.** Across sites,
  warm-season grasses green up earlier where spring is warmer and later where more of the
  rain falls in summer, and site climate predicts their typical green-up at a new site
  better than the ecoregion does. Cool-season curing follows the species and the site's
  wetness; warm-season curing dates are not explained by species, region or climate.
- **Place dominates.** Two-thirds to four-fifths of the variation in a grass's dates is
  where it grows and which species it is.
- **No weather model beats the typical date.** From one driver to a random forest, every
  model does as well as or worse than each grass's typical date, for green-up, curing and
  the cured date.
- **There is a shared year signal, mostly missed.** A quarter to two-fifths of the
  year-to-year variation is shared by the grasses at a site (about 18 days), mostly local to
  the site rather than region-wide. Moisture and summer vapour pressure deficit track it in the
  expected direction, but too weakly to predict it.
- **2016 and 2017 look different.** In those two years many NEON plants never reached
  their usual peak greenness, at most sites at once, which points to a change in how
  percent green was judged rather than weather. Leaving them out leaves every conclusion
  unchanged but removes about a third of the shared curing signal.

**Status (October 2026).**

| Component | Status |

| Series-years, climate metrics and site normals | Done |
| Model ladder (L0–L4), leave-one-year-out | Done |
| Variance partition (place, shared year, species, plant) | Done |
| Shared signal against local weather; managed and NEON sites | Done |

: Study status {.striped}

## Data and methods

### Data

- **Ground observations.** USA-NPN status and intensity records for grasses and sedges,
  2014–2024: on each visit the observer records, for a tagged plant, which class of "percent
  of the plant that is green" it is in (< 5, 5–24, 25–49, 50–74, 75–94, ≥ 95 %). 94 % of the
  plant-years come from the 36 NEON field sites, where technicians follow about five tagged
  plants per species; the rest are volunteer and managed sites. A plant-year is usable with at
  least 6 readings and a peak above 50 % green: 6,331 plant-years, 1,617 plants, 130 sites,
  70 species after crops (wheat, corn) are removed.
- **Grass types.** Each species is labelled cool-season (C3) or warm-season (C4), annual or
  perennial, and native or introduced, from the literature (72 species; under review with
  USA-NPN).
- **Climate.** PRISM daily 4 km precipitation, minimum and maximum temperature and maximum
  vapour pressure deficit, 2001–2025, at every site; site normals over 2002–2025.
- **Regions.** EPA / CEC Level II ecoregions (CEC 1997): the 130 sites fall in 17.

### Methods

- **Dates.** Green-up and curing are the dates a tagged plant passes 50 % green going up and
  coming down; the cured date is when it is fully cured. Crops (wheat, corn) are left out,
  and species are labeled C3 (cool-season) or C4 (warm-season) from the literature. Dates
  more than 90 days from the series' usual date count as a season mismatch and are not used.
- **Two sets of plants.** *The record, the typical dates and climate across space* use
  every plant-year with at least 6 readings and a peak above 50 % green (the NPN-derived
  "usable" curves), and a site and species with even one year: 6,331 plant-years. *The
  year-to-year analyses* need at least 12 readings per plant-year and 3 or more years per
  site and species: 707 series-years in 181 series (86 sites, 67 species), of which 289
  green-up, 529 curing and 461 cured series-years are scored. A series-year is one site,
  species and year, the median over that site-year's plants.
- **Typical date.** For each site and species, the circular median of its plants' dates
  over all years.
- **Regions.** EPA / Commission for Environmental Cooperation Level II ecoregions (CEC 1997),
  assigned to every site by its location; the 130 sites fall in 17 of them.
- **Weather.** Daily PRISM at each site, 2001–2025: growing degree-days, seasonal
  temperature, freeze dates, chilling, seasonal rain, vapour pressure deficit, rain events
  and dry spells, monsoon onset, and a moisture memory (a running average of daily
  precipitation minus potential evapotranspiration, over 15, 30 and 60 days). Each is used
  as a departure from the site's own average, so place is removed from both sides.
- **Two sets of curing drivers.** *Lead*: only weather known by the series' typical date
  minus 14 days (spring conditions, rain after the typical green-up, moisture memory and
  heat at that cutoff), the operational case. *Hindcast*: adds the summer and fall windows,
  which can run past the date.
- **The ladder**, the same data, folds and scores at each step:
  - **L0, typical date:** the series' average over the training years. This is the bar.
  - **L1, one driver:** March–April temperature for green-up; moisture memory at the cutoff
    (lead) or June–August rain (hindcast) for curing.
  - **L2, process rule:** green-up when growing degree-days reach the series' usual amount;
    curing when the 30-day moisture memory falls below the series' usual level and stays
    there (within 60 days of the typical date), or at the first hard fall freeze if earlier.
  - **L3, regression:** up to four drivers chosen by forward selection, per C3/C4.
  - **L4, random forest:** all drivers plus site climate, pathway and life cycle.
- **Scoring.** Leave one year out (every series loses the same year at once). Mean absolute
  error in days; skill = 1 − error / error of the typical date; and the correlation of each
  model's predicted departure with the observed one.

## The record

| | Plant-years | Plants | Sites | Species | Readings | Dated: green-up / curing / cured |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All usable curves | 6,331 | 1,617 | 130 | 70 | 203,290 | 2,638 / 4,611 / 3,361 |
| NEON field sites | 5,960 | 1,438 | 36 | 56 | 195,630 | 2,478 / 4,411 / 3,178 |
| Other NPN sites | 371 | 179 | 94 | 34 | 7,660 | 160 / 200 / 183 |
| Year-to-year set (≥ 12 readings, ≥ 3 years) | 5,668 | 1,417 | 48 | 60 | 195,405 | 2,514 / 4,385 / 3,171 |

: The NPN grass percent-green record, 2014–2024 {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-sites}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_sites",
  "Where the NPN grass curing study sites are. Filled points are NEON field sites, which hold 94 % of the plant-years; open points are other NPN sites. Point size is the number of plant-years.",
  "Map of the contiguous U.S. with NPN grass study sites coloured by cool-season, warm-season or both grass types, sized by plant-years, filled for NEON sites.")
```

```{r fig-npn-record}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_record",
  "What the record is made of: the percent-green class of each reading, how many readings each plant-year carries, and how often a plant greens up a second time after curing, by region.",
  "Three panels: horizontal bars of reading shares by percent-green class; box summaries of readings per plant-year for NEON, other and managed sites; bars of second green-up share by region.")
```

- **NEON carries the record.** 94 % of plant-years, and 96 % of the readings, come from the
  36 NEON sites. Their plants are read about weekly through most of the year (median 35
  readings per plant-year). The other 94 sites are read just as often while observed, but
  over shorter spans (median 14–16 readings), so they add places, not years: in the
  year-to-year set they are only 16 sites.
- **The whole scale is used.** A third of all readings are in the top class (95 % green or
  more); each of the other classes holds 10–20 %.
- **Second green-ups are common.** 18 % of plant-years fall below 25 % green and then come
  back above 50 % at least three weeks later (cool-season 15 %, warm-season 19 %), most often
  in Mediterranean California (44 %, the annual grasses greening again with the first fall
  rains within the same calendar year), the Mississippi Alluvial and Southeast USA Coastal
  Plains (35 %), the Southeastern USA Plains (27 %) and the Warm Deserts (27 %). In 276 plant-years the 50 % curing date belongs to the second cycle.
- **Some plants never pass 50 % green.** 6 % of NEON plant-years with enough readings stay
  below 50 % all year, so they have no green-up or curing date. Almost all are in 2016 and
  2017 (see [the check below](#a-check-2016-and-2017)).

## When grasses green up and cure

```{r fig-npn-dates}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_dates",
  "Typical green-up, 50 % curing and cured dates by EPA Level II ecoregion and grass type. Each point is one site and species (its typical date over all years observed); the bar is the region median where it has three or more.",
  "Three panels of dot plots: green-up, curing and cured dates by ecoregion, cool-season grasses in blue and warm-season in orange.")
```

- **The season moves with ecoregion and grass type.** Warm-season grasses on the Mississippi
  Alluvial and Southeast USA Coastal Plains (8.5) green up in late February and cure around
  October 20; in the Warm Deserts (10.2) they green up with the summer rains in late June and cure
  at the end of September. Cool-season grasses cure in mid-May in Mediterranean California
  (11.1), late June in the Cold Deserts (10.1) and late July in the Western Cordillera (6.2),
  and from early August (South Central Semiarid Prairies, 9.4) to late September (West-Central
  Semiarid Prairies, 9.3) on the Great Plains.
- **Cool- versus warm-season depends on the region.** Where both are observed in three or
  more series each, warm-season grasses cure 38 days later than cool-season ones in the South
  Central Semiarid Prairies (9.4) and 75 days later in the Cold Deserts (10.1); on the
  Southeastern USA Plains (8.3) cool-season grasses green up 75 days earlier and cure 29 days
  later. In the Mixed Wood Plains (8.1) and West-Central Semiarid Prairies (9.3) the two types
  differ by less than three weeks.
- **Annual grasses cure early.** In the Cold Deserts annual grasses (mostly cheatgrass) cure
  77 days earlier than perennial cool-season grasses, and in the Western Cordillera 97 days
  earlier (3 annual series each).
- **Small cells need care.** Many ecoregion and grass-type combinations rest on 2–5 sites;
  cool-season green-up in early August in the Western Cordillera (three series) reflects
  mountain sites, and single points in other cells may be fall green-ups.

## Do typical dates follow site climate?

Each site and species' typical date was modelled on the site's climate normals (PRISM,
2002–2025), with a random effect for species, and compared with a model of species alone,
one with the ecoregion instead of climate, and one with both. Climate is a small set
chosen in advance: March–April mean temperature for green-up, July–August mean temperature
for curing, and for both aridity (precipitation / potential evapotranspiration), the share
of rain falling July–September and latitude. Each model is scored by refitting it with one
site left out at a time and predicting that site.

| Date | Grass type | Series (sites) | Species only | Ecoregion | Site climate | Ecoregion + climate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | warm-season (C4) | 115 (66) | 0.39 | 0.40 | **0.61** | 0.59 |
| Green-up | cool-season (C3) | 36 (25) | −0.23 | 0.15 | 0.19 | below −1 |
| 50 % curing | warm-season (C4) | 123 (61) | 0.02 | −0.10 | 0.00 | −0.13 |
| 50 % curing | cool-season (C3) | 62 (38) | **0.63** | 0.59 | **0.63** | 0.04 |
| Cured | warm-season (C4) | 110 (56) | −0.10 | −0.10 | −0.01 | −0.17 |
| Cured | cool-season (C3) | 58 (34) | **0.65** | 0.59 | 0.64 | 0.04 |

: Share of the variation in typical dates predicted at a site left out (R², 0 = no better than the mean) {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-spatial}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_spatial",
  "Typical dates against site climate. Left: how well each model (species only, ecoregion, site climate, both) predicts a left-out site. Middle: typical green-up against March–April temperature. Right: typical 50 % curing against site aridity.",
  "Three panels: dot chart of leave-one-site-out R-squared for four models, three dates and three grass groups; scatter of green-up date against spring temperature; scatter of curing date against aridity.")
```

- **Warm-season green-up follows site climate,** better than the ecoregion does: about
  38 days earlier per standard deviation of warmer March–April temperature, and 27 days
  later per standard deviation more of the rain in summer (the monsoon sites green up with
  the summer rains).
- **Cool-season green-up tracks spring temperature too** (rank correlation about −0.8 to
  −0.9 depending on the series included), but with 25 sites the models do not hold up at a
  left-out site.
- **Cool-season curing and the cured date follow the species about as well as the climate.**
  Wetter sites, and sites with more summer rain, cure 20–25 days later per standard
  deviation; but which species grow where already carries most of that.
- **Warm-season curing and cured dates are not explained across sites** by species, region
  or climate.
- **Adding the ecoregion to the climate overfits.** With 17 ecoregions and a few dozen sites
  per grass type, ecoregion plus climate does worse at a left-out site than climate alone.
- The same holds, more weakly, in the stricter year-to-year set.

## Can weather beat the typical date?

| Date | Series-years | Typical-date error | L1 | L2 | L3 | L4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 289 | 24.8 days | 0.00 | −0.04 | −0.02 | −0.02 |
| 50 % curing | 529 | 27.6 days | 0.00 | −0.33 | −0.04 | −0.02 |
| Cured | 461 | 23.7 days | +0.01 | −0.17 | −0.05 | −0.03 |

: Skill against the typical date (0 = no better, negative = worse), lead driver set {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-ladder}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_ladder",
  "Skill of each model against the typical date (0 = no better, negative = worse), lead driver set, leave-one-year-out. Black: all grasses; blue: cool-season; orange: warm-season.",
  "Dot charts of skill for four model levels and three dates; all points sit at or below zero.")
```

- **No step beats the typical date.** The best is one driver for the cured date (+0.01,
  correlation 0.15). The process rules, the regression and the random forest all add
  error. The same holds for C3 and C4 separately, in each region with enough data, when
  species are averaged within a site-year, and with the hindcast drivers that can see
  past the date.
- **The regression does not settle on drivers.** Its choices change from one left-out
  year to the next.
- **The ceiling is low.** Species observed at the same site in the same year share only
  part of their early or late year: 22 % of the year-to-year variance for green-up, 24 %
  for curing and 40 % for the cured date. The rest is specific to the plant or the
  observer, which no weather record can explain.

## How much of the year-to-year variation could weather explain?

To measure the ceiling directly, each plant's date is split into parts with a mixed model
on all plant-years (5,780 plant-years, 1,514 plants, 84 sites; plant dates more than 90 days
from the series' usual date, 5–10 %, are left out): place (site, species, and
the species at that site), a year signal shared by the grasses at a site (national,
regional and site-wide), a year signal of one species at one site, and what is left for
the single plant.

| Date | Plant-years | Place, % of all variation | Year-to-year SD | Shared by the site's grasses | Region-wide part of that | One species only | Single plant |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Green-up | 2,563 | 70 % | 30 days | 37 % | 12 % | 24 % | 40 % |
| 50 % curing | 4,468 | 71 % | 36 days | 28 % | 14 % | 20 % | 52 % |
| Cured | 3,225 | 80 % | 30 days | 39 % | 8 % | 22 % | 39 % |

: Variance partition of NPN grass dates; the last four columns are shares of the year-to-year variation {.striped}

```{r fig-npn-variance}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_variance",
  "What the year-to-year variation in each date is made of: shared across the region, shared by the grasses at a site, specific to one species at a site, or specific to the single plant.",
  "Stacked horizontal bars of the four shares for green-up, curing and cured, all grasses and by grass type.")
```

- **Place dominates.** 70–80 % of the variation in a plant's date is where
  it grows and what species it is. That is what the typical-date maps carry.
- **Of the year-to-year part, 28–39 % is shared** by the grasses at a site:
  about 18 days (standard deviation) for each date. That shared part is the most any
  weather record at the site could explain, and the ladder above explained almost none of
  it. So the ceiling is real but not zero: the weather drivers tried so far miss a
  shared signal that exists.
- **Little of it is region-wide.** Within an ecoregion, the part every site shares is 12 %
  of green-up's year-to-year variation, 14 % of curing's and 8 % of the cured date's; most of
  the shared signal is local to the site. Local weather is one explanation; so are things that
  act on a whole site in a year, such as mowing, grazing, irrigation or a change of observer,
  which the data cannot separate.
- **Half of the year-to-year variation in 50 % curing belongs to the single plant**,
  more for warm-season (C4) grasses (62 %) than cool-season (C3, 37 %). The spacing of
  readings accounts for only 1–3 % of it, so it is not a sampling artefact: plants of one
  species at one site really differ (microsite, age, how each observer judges "percent
  green").
- **Averaging the plants helps but does not remove it.** In a site-species-year mean
  (median 3–5 plants) the shared part is about half (48–55 %) of the year-to-year variation.

## Does the shared signal follow local weather?

The shared part was estimated for each
site-year from the same model (203–290 site-years at 64–71 sites) and compared with that
year's weather departures at the site.

- **For curing and the cured date it does, weakly, and in the expected direction.** Sites with
  more summer rain events or lower summer vapour pressure deficit cure later (correlations
  about 0.15–0.25; strongest: June–August VPD, April–September rain events, and VPD in the 30
  days before the typical date).
- **But not enough to predict it.** Fitted on the other years, a selected set of drivers
  explains none of the shared signal in a left-out year. So most of the site-wide year signal is something the 4 km weather record
  does not see: very local weather and soil, or what happens at the site (mowing, grazing,
  irrigation, a new observer).
```{r fig-npn-signal}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_signal",
  "The shared site-year signal against June–August vapour pressure deficit, both as departures within each year: higher summer VPD goes with earlier curing, but the scatter is wide.",
  "Two scatter plots with a downward-sloping fitted line, curing and cured.")
```

- **Managed sites are not the explanation.** Gardens, yards, campuses and parks are only
  about 4 % of the usable plant-years, too few to fit on their own; the results without them
  are unchanged.
- **The year-to-year record is mostly NEON.** 96 % of the plant-years in this set come from
  the 36 National Ecological Observatory Network field sites, where trained technicians
  follow five tagged plants per species in natural plots. Results without NEON sites are too
  thin to compare (124–154 plant-years). So the large plant share is not volunteer noise: it is real
  plant-to-plant variation within a plot plus how each technician judges "percent green",
  and the site-wide year signal may include crew changes and visit schedules as well as
  weather.
- **For green-up, the links are with summer temperature, after the event,** so they reflect
  which years were warm overall rather than a cause, and they do not carry over to a
  left-out year either.

## A check: 2016 and 2017

In most years about 1 % of NEON plant-years never pass 50 % green. In 2016 it was 16 % and
in 2017 30 %, at 11 of the 18 NEON sites observed then; in those two years only 53 % of
plant-years reached the top class (95 % green or more), against 89 % in other years. A
change that shows up at most sites at once, in two consecutive years, points to how
percent green was judged rather than to weather. A plant that peaks lower crosses 50 % on
the way down earlier, so those years could look like early-curing years everywhere.

```{r fig-npn-sensitivity}
#| results: asis
show_fig("npn_sensitivity",
  "Left: share of NEON plant-years that never pass 50 % green, by year. Right: the share of the year-to-year variation shared by a site's grasses, with all years and without 2016–2017.",
  "Bar chart by year with 2016 and 2017 standing out; paired bars for green-up, curing and cured.")
```

| | All years | Without 2016–17 |
|---|---|---|
| Best model skill against the typical date: green-up / curing / cured | 0.00 / 0.00 / +0.01 | +0.02 / 0.00 / +0.01 |
| Shared by the site's grasses (% of year-to-year): green-up | 37 % | 28 % |
| — 50 % curing | 28 % | 20 % |
| — cured | 39 % | 38 % |
| Region-wide part: green-up / curing / cured | 12 / 14 / 8 % | 15 / 6 / 10 % |

: The year-to-year results with and without 2016–2017 (series-years and plant-years in those years dropped) {.striped}

- **The conclusions do not change.** Nothing beats the typical date either way.
- **But more than a quarter of the shared curing signal was 2016–17.** Without them, the year
  signal shared by a site's grasses is 20 % of the year-to-year variation in 50 % curing rather
  than 28 %; the cured date is unaffected, as expected if those years mostly lowered the
  peak.
- **Without them, curing follows moisture more clearly.** Wetter years cure later, with
  correlations of about 0.22 for annual rain, April–September rain events and the 60-day
  moisture memory (23 of 61 drivers significant, against 2 with all years), yet still too
  weakly to predict a left-out year.
- The main results keep all years; this check is reported alongside until USA-NPN and NEON
  can say whether guidance or training for percent green changed around 2018.

## What it means so far

On the ground, as with the satellite rules on the [regions page](index.html), the typical
date is the baseline to beat, and so far nothing beats it. The typical date itself is
predictable for green-up, which follows site climate, and much less so for curing, which
follows the species for cool-season grasses and nothing measured here for warm-season
ones. There is a shared year signal, mostly local to the site, that
moisture and VPD track only weakly; part of the curing signal looks like a 2016–17 change
in how plants were judged. A first check with the PhenoCam cameras at the NEON plots was
not a fair test: the camera transition dates skip years with a weak green-up, mark a
different stage of the season (the end of the spring flush rather than half-cured plants),
and switch between seasons at sites that green up twice. A comparison based on camera
greenness around each site's typical curing date would avoid those problems; it is on hold.

## Toward a paper

A draft outline, framed as a data and methods paper. Title idea: *Grass green-up and curing on
the ground: a national record from NEON and USA-NPN percent-green observations*.

**Contribution.** The first national ground record of when U.S. grasses green up and cure, by
ecoregion and grass type; evidence that typical green-up follows site climate while typical
curing largely does not; and evidence that weather adds no skill over the typical date from
year to year, with the reason (most of the year-to-year scatter belongs to single plants).
The typical date is therefore the baseline for grass fuel monitoring, and any weather
adjustment has to beat it on ground data. ("First" still needs a literature check.)

1. **Introduction.** Curing is the grass fuel variable fire managers need and has almost no
   ground record in the U.S.; NPN's percent-green question is, in practice, a curing
   measurement.
2. **Data and methods.** The record and its filters; curve dates; C3 / C4 and life-cycle
   labels; PRISM metrics and normals; ecoregions; typical dates, spatial models, variance
   partition, model ladder.
3. **The record (Q1).** Size and coverage, reading density, use of the percent-green classes,
   second green-ups, plants that never pass 50 %. Figures: site map, record.
4. **Typical dates (Q2).** By ecoregion and grass type; cool- versus warm-season and annual
   versus perennial contrasts. Figure: dates by ecoregion.
5. **What sets the typical date across sites (Q4).** Green-up follows site climate; cool-season
   curing follows the species; warm-season curing is unexplained. Figure: spatial.
6. **Year to year (Q3, Q5, Q6).** Place dominates; a small shared year signal tracked weakly by
   moisture; no model beats the typical date, simple process rules included. Figures:
   variance, ladder, shared signal.
7. **Data quality: 2016–2017.** What it is and what it changes (pending USA-NPN / NEON).
8. **Discussion.** The typical date as the baseline for fire danger; why prediction from year to
   year is capped; why warm-season curing resists explanation; recommendations for monitoring
   (read through the end of the season, the same plants for several years, several plants per
   species, wildland sites, clearer percent-green guidance).
9. **Conclusions.**

Supplement: filter funnel, the stricter year-to-year set as a sensitivity, the C3 / C4 table,
per-ecoregion tables. Open: venue (*International Journal of Wildland Fire*, *Fire*, a
phenology or data journal), co-authors from USA-NPN, whether to invite NEON, and whether the
PhenoCam comparison earns a place.

## Decisions so far

| Date | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Oct 11 2026 | Scope: NPN "percent green" records for grasses with daily PRISM; no GSI, no soil data | Curing measured directly; mapped soil is unlikely to describe the soil under a tagged plant |
| Oct 11 2026 | Moisture as a running P − PET memory (15, 30, 60 days) instead of a soil bucket | Carries wet and dry spells without a soil parameter |
| Oct 15 2026 | A companion study to the regions work, with its own page; code shared with the regions work | Reuses the PRISM, cue and region code; region numbers match the maps |
| Oct 15 2026 | Cool- and warm-season (C3/C4) assigned by species from the literature, to be reviewed with USA-NPN | No national C3/C4 grass layer |
| Oct 15 2026 | At least 12 readings per plant-year; series need 3 or more years; dates more than 90 days from a series' usual date counted as a season mismatch | Enough readings to place the crossings; mismatches would dominate the errors |
| Oct 15 2026 | Likely managed sites flagged and reported both ways | Gardens and yards may not follow local weather |
| Oct 16 2026 | Normals over 2002–2025 | Daily PRISM used here starts in 2001 |
| Oct 16 2026 | No other plant groups (forbs, shrubs) and no NEON observer or tower-sensor tests | Other groups answer a different percent question; keep the study focused |
| Oct 16 2026 | Two sets: every usable curve (≥ 6 readings, any number of years) for the record, typical dates and climate across space; ≥ 12 readings and ≥ 3 years for the year-to-year analyses | Short volunteer series still give typical dates; year-to-year needs repeated years |
| Oct 16 2026 | NPN-derived "usable" rule (≥ 6 readings, peak above 50 % green) left as is | Sparser volunteer records cannot place a crossing |
| Oct 16 2026 | 2016–2017 reported as a sensitivity check; main results keep all years | Likely a judging change, not yet confirmed with USA-NPN and NEON |
| Oct 18 2026 | EPA Level II ecoregions for all region results | A published regionalization, independent of the fuel phenology regions (which were chosen partly on these ground dates) |
| Oct 16 2026 | Second green-up: below 25 % green, then above 50 % on two readings at least three weeks later | A looser rule mostly caught readings flickering around 50 % |

: Study decisions {.striped}
